vignette: John, a 54-year-old European American civil servant, has been experiencing significant distress following physical abuse by his romantic partner. The traumatic event occurred two years ago and marked a turning point in John's life, leading to a cascade of symptoms that have progressively eroded his sense of safety and control. The night of the trauma was particularly brutal for John. He had come home from work late one evening, only to find his partner waiting for him with an expression of anger and frustration. As he entered their shared living space, the tension in the room escalated quickly into a violent confrontation. His partner attacked him without warning, leaving John both physically injured and deeply shaken by the loss of control over the situation. Since that night, John's life has been marked by constant vigilance and an overwhelming fear of losing control again. He finds himself acutely aware of his surroundings at all times, especially in situations where he perceives a lack of safety or support. For instance, when alone in their home late at night, John experiences intense anxiety, often leading him to sleep separately from his partner as a coping mechanism. This decision has strained their relationship, with his partner feeling isolated and unheard. John's work environment, which requires him to interact with colleagues on a daily basis, also presents challenges. He has become particularly sensitive to the presence of men in close proximity, especially when he is alone in an office or building. He avoids situations where he might be alone with male colleagues, often finding excuses to leave meetings early or delegating tasks that require private interactions. In an effort to manage his anxiety and detachment from painful memories, John has developed several maladaptive strategies. One of these is constantly socializing, which allows him to stay in environments filled with people so he never has to be alone with his thoughts. He often spends late hours at the office or engages in group activities outside work, finding solace in the company of others. However, this constant need for social interaction has started to affect his productivity and professional relationships. Colleagues have noticed his frequent absences from meetings and his reluctance to take on solo tasks, leading to subtle but growing tensions at work. John feels caught between needing the support of others and being overwhelmed by the demands it places on him. John's memory of the traumatic event is fragmented yet vivid in certain aspects. When he tries to deliberately recall what happened that night, he finds it difficult to access the memory clearly; instead, it feels disjointed and vague. However, when triggered, the memories flood back with photographic clarity, as if he were reliving every moment through a series of still images in his mind. This vividness is further heightened by sensory details, such as the taste he associates with that night, which can suddenly return without warning. The cumulative impact of these symptoms has led John to seek help, driven by an increasing sense of isolation and fear that things will only get worse if left unchecked. He fears losing his job due to frequent absences and feels a growing distance from his partner, who struggles to understand why he withdraws into constant socializing rather than discussing their shared life. John hopes for a way to regain control over his thoughts and emotions without having to rely on avoidance or detachment. He is eager to find strategies that can help him confront the traumatic memories in a manageable way, ultimately seeking to rebuild trust and stability in both his personal and professional relationships.
